passages.text: On the next day, then, Peter, who was about to debate with Simon, woke rather early and prayed. Just as he finished, Zacchaeus came in and said, “Simon is sitting outside, speaking with some of his own people, about thirty of them.” Peter said, “Let him speak until a crowd gathers, and then let us begin the debate. In this way we can hear what he says, prepare ourselves to address it, and go out and speak.” And that is what happened. Zacchaeus went out and, not long afterward, came back in and reported to Peter the statements Simon had made against Peter.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can denote comparison or putting statements before someone; reported fits the messenger’s relay of Simon’s speech, not a second debate with Peter.

passages.text: He said, “He accuses you, Peter, of being a servant of evil, of having great power in magic, and of filling people’s souls with images in a way worse than idolatry. He seemed to offer this as proof that you are a magician, saying: ‘I know about myself that I think things through when I am alone, but when I come to debate with him, I do not remember a single argument. For while he is speaking, my mind is occupied with recalling the things I had thought of saying to him when I came, and I do not hear anything at all that he says. Since I do not experience anything like this with anyone else, but only with him, how am I not being bewitched by him? That whatever he teaches is worse than idolatry will be clear to anyone with understanding once I explain it. For there is no other benefit than for the soul to become free of idols of every kind. When it imagines a form, it is bound by fear; it withers with anxiety about suffering something, and, being altered, becomes possessed. Yet in its possession it seems to most people to be sound-minded.

lexical_decisions.rationale: This is Simon’s reported accusation, not the narrator’s verdict. ὑπηρέτης is an assistant or subordinate.
Preserves the mental-image vocabulary that structures Simon’s criticism, not generic deception alone.
The bracketed letters already belong to the supplied edition’s reading. No new restoration is made.
Retains the demon/possession language; raves or acts like one possessed is a possible phenomenological rendering.

passages.text: This is what Peter gives you under a promise of making you sound-minded. For under the pretext of one God he seems to free you from many lifeless idols. These do not do their worshipers much harm, because with their very eyes they can see that they are stone, bronze, gold, or some other lifeless material. Therefore, knowing that what is seen is nothing, the soul cannot be haunted by fear in the same way through the visible thing. But when, through deceptive teaching, it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition. I say these things not because I advise you to revere idols, but because Peter, while seeming to free your souls from fearsome ideas, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome idea, introducing a God with a form—and, moreover, supremely just. With this comes terror, and shuddering for the soul that thinks of it, capable even of loosening the tension of sound reasoning. For the mind, placed in such a storm, has its brightness muddied like deep water by a violent wind. Therefore, if he comes for your benefit, let him not, while seeming to dissolve your relatively mild fears arising from lifeless forms, introduce in their place a fearsome form of God. But does God have a form? If he does, he has a shape. If he has a shape, how is he not bounded? If bounded, he is in a place. If in a place, he is less than the place containing him. If less than something, how is he greater, stronger, or higher than all? So much for these matters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς φοβερὸν θεὸν ἀποβλέπουσα τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the upheaval/derangement image and the author’s contrast with nature; this remains Simon’s reported position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὀρθῶν λογισμῶν ἐκλῦσαι τοὺς τόνους
lexical_decisions.chosen: loosening the tension of sound reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the tension image rather than merely saying it makes thinking difficult.
Keeps distinct vocabulary in the chain of argument. Bounded denotes spatial delimitation, not simply weakness.

passages.text: It is also obvious that he does not truly believe even the things said by his own teacher, for he proclaims the opposite of them. For, as I learn, his teacher said to someone, “Do not call me good, for the good one is one.” In saying good, he does not mean that just one whom the scriptures proclaim, who kills and gives life—kills those who sin and gives life to those who live according to his judgment. That he really did not call the maker good is clear to anyone able to think it through. For the maker was known to Adam, whom he formed; to Enoch, who pleased him; to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous; likewise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and also to Moses, the people, and the whole world. Yet Peter’s teacher Jesus came and said, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore, if the one present was himself the Son, from his coming he revealed to those he wished the one unknown to all. Thus the Father was unknown to everyone before him, not being this one who was known to all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν, ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not call me good, for the good one is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the wording actually quoted here, not a familiar expanded Gospel form. Simon’s distinction between good and just is retained as his argument.
δημιουργός denotes creator or maker, not automatically an evil demiurge; the speaker’s proposed distinction is not editorially endorsed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δικαίῳ ὁραθέντι Νῶε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Noah, whom he saw to be righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes Noah as the one seen as righteous by God; it is not inverted into Noah seeing God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinct Greek knew/knows forms instead of homogenizing the quoted tenses.

passages.text: And in saying this, Jesus does not even agree with himself. For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God, saying, “Do not fear the one who kills the body but can do nothing to the soul. Fear the one who can cast both body and soul into the Gehenna of fire. Yes, I tell you, fear this one.” That he really said to fear this one as a just God, to whom he also says the wronged should cry out, is shown when he gives a parable on this and adds its explanation, saying, “If, then, the unjust judge acted in this way because he was petitioned repeatedly, how much more will the Father bring vindication for those who cry to him day and night? Or do you think that because he is patient with them, he will not do it? Yes, I tell you, he will do it, and quickly.” But whoever says that God vindicates and repays establishes him as just by nature, and not good. Further, he also gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth. If he is Lord of heaven and earth, he is acknowledged as maker; and being maker, he is just. Calling him good at one time and just at another, he does not agree even in this way. Thirdly, his wise disciple insisted yesterday that direct perception is more adequate than an apparition, not knowing that direct perception can be human, whereas an apparition is acknowledged to belong to divinity.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the named place and fire qualification, not the distinct Hades term.
ἐκδίκησις can be vengeance or the securing of justice. Vindication fits the wronged petitioners while retaining the punitive repayment explained afterward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: direct perception is more adequate than an apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνάργεια here is direct evident encounter, contrasted with ὀπτασία, an apparition. The polemical wise disciple is not softened into neutral description.
